passage_title: Cloudiness in the Wells at Ferrin Flat
passage:
Six wells at Ferrin Flat draw water from one body of sand about 30 m below the surface. Beneath the sand lies a layer of clay, separated from the sand by about 2 m of gravel. Each well is lined with a steel casing.

Water from the wells was clear until 2019. Since then it has been cloudy, and the cloudiness is caused by a fine pale solid suspended in the water. Several observations have been recorded. The cloudiness first appeared within a month of the deepening of Well 3. The four cloudiest wells are the four whose casings were installed in 1974; the two least cloudy are the two cased in 2011. A jar of the water left standing for 24 hr is still cloudy. The suspended solid is 19% by mass a metal that is also the main metal of the casings. When a pump is started, turbidity rises for about 90 s and then settles to a steady value about one-third as high.

Two scientists explain the cloudiness.

Scientist 1

The solid comes from the clay. Deepening Well 3 carried its borehole down through the gravel and into the clay. Pumping any of the six wells lowers the water level across the whole body of sand, and the water that moves in to replace it now passes out of the clay, through the gravel, and into the sand, carrying the finest clay particles with it. Those particles are fine enough to pass between the gravel grains and too fine to settle out of a jar in a day. Clay of this kind holds the metal in question within itself, so a solid made of clay carries that metal at about the measured fraction with none of it coming from a casing. The four cloudiest wells are simply the four that sit nearest the path the water takes from Well 3; their casings happen to be the old ones, and their age has nothing to do with it. The rise in turbidity over the first 90 s is particles that had settled inside the well between pumpings being lifted again. Line the length of Well 3 that passes through the clay and the cloudiness will end in all six wells.

Scientist 2

The solid comes from the casings. A steel casing corrodes wherever water and air both reach it, and the corrosion product is a fine pale solid that stays suspended for days. That is why the solid carries the casing metal, and why the four wells cased in 1974 are the four cloudiest while the two cased in 2011 are the clearest. Deepening Well 3 opened no path to the clay. What it did was lower the water level in every well by about 3 m, exposing a band of each casing about 3 m tall to air for the first time. A casing corrodes far faster on that newly exposed band than it does below the water, which is why the change followed the deepening so closely. The rise in turbidity over the first 90 s is flakes shed from the exposed band into the standing water of the well. Lining Well 3 will change nothing; the casings must be replaced.
prompt: Both scientists would most likely agree with which of the following statements about the wells at Ferrin Flat?
choices: The deepening of Well 3 opened a path from the clay into the body of sand.
Replacing the casings of all six wells would put an end to the cloudiness in every one of them.
The pale solid in the water contains a metal that is also present in the casings.
The age of a well’s casing has nothing to do with how cloudy that well is.
correct_answer: The pale solid in the water contains a metal that is also present in the casings.
explanation: Both accounts have to explain the measurement that the suspended solid is 19% by mass a metal that is also the main metal of the casings, and neither disputes it: Scientist 2 says the solid is corroded casing, and Scientist 1 says clay of this kind "holds the metal in question within itself." The other statements each belong to one account alone. Opening "a path from the clay into the body of sand" is what Scientist 2 denies ("Deepening Well 3 opened no path to the clay"); replacing the casings is Scientist 2’s remedy, which Scientist 1 would expect to fail; and "the age of a well’s casing has nothing to do with how cloudy that well is" is Scientist 1’s reading of the age correlation, which Scientist 2 treats as the central evidence.

passage:

In a second set of trials, a 2 mm thick panel and an 8 mm thick panel of each blend were molded at 80 °C and their warp measured in the same way. The results are shown in Figure 2.

passage_title: Warp of Molded Panels Made from Four Resin Blends
passage:
Panels were molded from four resin blends, labeled Blend W, Blend X, Blend Y, and Blend Z. A molded panel does not cool perfectly flat; the greatest distance between the cooled panel and a flat reference plate is called the warp of that panel. All panels were molded from the same mass of resin, in the same mold, and were cooled in still air at 20 °C.

In one set of trials, a 4 mm thick panel of each blend was molded at each of five mold temperatures, and the warp of each panel was measured. The results are shown in Figure 1.

In a second set of trials, a 2 mm thick panel and an 8 mm thick panel of each blend were molded at 80 °C and their warp measured in the same way. The results are shown in Figure 2.

choices: less than 0.55 mm.
between 0.55 mm and 0.95 mm.

explanation: Over the last stretch of the Blend Z curve the warp is falling steeply, from about 1.15 mm at 100 °C to about 0.55 mm at 120 °C. Continuing that fall past 120 °C puts a 140 °C panel below 0.55 mm. Each of the other ranges would require the curve either to level off or to turn back upward within the next 20 °C, and nothing in the measured part of the Blend Z curve shows it doing so at that end.
